problem.statement_clinical: Asthma, childhood diagnosis, no current symptoms or inhaler

subjective.vernacular: In the past year, have you noticed any whistling or squeaky sound when you breathe?
subjective.why_it_matters: Current wheeze would support active or persistent asthma rather than remission.

subjective.vernacular: Do you get short of breath, chest tightness, or start coughing during or just after exercise?
subjective.why_it_matters: Exercise-induced symptoms are the most common residual pattern in adult patients with childhood asthma and distinguish active from remitted disease.

subjective.vernacular: Do you wake up at night because of coughing, chest tightness, or trouble breathing?
subjective.why_it_matters: Nocturnal symptoms are a hallmark of uncontrolled or persistent asthma.

subjective.vernacular: Have you had a cough that has lasted more than 3 weeks without a clear cold or infection causing it?
subjective.why_it_matters: Cough-variant asthma can present with isolated chronic cough in the absence of wheeze or dyspnea.

subjective.vernacular: Do you have hay fever — sneezing, runny nose, or itchy eyes triggered by pollen, dust, or animals?
subjective.why_it_matters: Allergic rhinitis is strongly associated with atopic asthma and its persistence into adulthood; a runny nose symptom was noted 2026-06-14.
subjective.value: Runny nose noted 2026-06-14 (mild); unclear if allergic or infectious
subjective.missing: Chronicity, triggers, and relationship to allergen exposure not documented

subjective.vernacular: Have you ever had eczema — itchy, dry, or scaly skin patches that come and go?
subjective.why_it_matters: Eczema is part of the atopic triad and increases the likelihood that childhood asthma was allergic and may persist.

subjective.vernacular: Does your breathing get worse around pets, dust, smoke, strong smells, cold air, or mold?
subjective.why_it_matters: Identifiable triggers suggest ongoing airway hyperresponsiveness consistent with active asthma.

subjective.term: Tobacco smoke exposure — current or historical
subjective.vernacular: Do you smoke now, or did you smoke in the past? Are you regularly around other people who smoke?
subjective.why_it_matters: Smoking or secondhand smoke worsens airway obstruction and complicates differentiating asthma from COPD in adulthood.

subjective.vernacular: Have you ever noticed that ibuprofen or aspirin made your breathing worse?
subjective.why_it_matters: NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease is a distinct asthma phenotype; ibuprofen is listed as a current medication.
subjective.value: Ibuprofen listed as active OTC medication (2026-07-01); respiratory response not documented
subjective.missing: Whether ibuprofen use has triggered respiratory symptoms

subjective.vernacular: How old were you when you were diagnosed with asthma, and what treatments did you use — inhalers, nebulizers, pills?
subjective.why_it_matters: Age of onset, severity, and treatment history help predict whether asthma has remitted or is likely to recur.

subjective.vernacular: How long has it been since you last had any asthma symptoms or needed an inhaler?
subjective.why_it_matters: A prolonged symptom-free period without treatment supports clinical remission.

subjective.term: Dyspnea at rest or with low exertion
subjective.vernacular: Do you ever feel short of breath while sitting still or doing very light activity like walking slowly?
subjective.why_it_matters: Resting dyspnea would suggest a more severe or alternative respiratory diagnosis.

subjective.vernacular: Do you have frequent heartburn, acid coming up into your throat, or a sour taste in your mouth?
subjective.why_it_matters: GERD is a common cause of chronic cough and airway hyperresponsiveness that can mimic or exacerbate asthma.

subjective.vernacular: Does your work or home environment expose you to dust, chemicals, fumes, animals, or mold?
subjective.why_it_matters: Occupational exposures can cause new-onset or recurrent adult asthma independent of childhood history.

objective.vernacular: Breathing test measuring how much and how fast air can be blown out, before and after a bronchodilator inhaler
Measurement of the fastest speed at which air can be blown out of the lungs
objective.how_obtained: Peak flow meter — clinic or home

objective.vernacular: Percentage of oxygen carried in the blood, measured by a finger sensor
Listening to the lungs with a stethoscope to detect wheeze, prolonged expiration, or reduced air entry

objective.term: Chest wall inspection — accessory muscle use
objective.vernacular: Looking at the chest and neck for signs that extra muscles are being used to breathe
A number calculated from height and weight that estimates healthy weight range
objective.how_obtained: Calculated from measured height and weight
objective.value: Weight 185 lbs (83.9 kg) on 2026-06-14; height 220 cm (2021) — BMI approx 17.4 (possibly data quality issue given prior 'overweight' diagnosis)
objective.missing: Accurate current height measurement to confirm BMI; 220 cm height is physiologically unusual and may be a data entry error

objective.vernacular: A breath test that measures airway inflammation — high levels suggest allergic-type asthma
An X-ray image of the chest to look at the lungs and airways
objective.value: Chest X-ray 2 views performed 2023-06-02; results not available in record

objective.term: Serum total IgE and allergen-specific IgE (RAST) panel
objective.vernacular: Blood tests showing whether the immune system is reacting to common allergens like dust mites, pollen, or pet dander
A blood cell count that measures a type of immune cell that is elevated in allergic and eosinophilic asthma
A test that checks whether the airways are extra-sensitive by having the person inhale a substance that can cause mild narrowing
Assessment of whether PCOS (diagnosed 2005) is being managed, given its association with obesity and systemic inflammation
objective.how_obtained: Review of existing diagnosis and current management
objective.value: PCOS diagnosed 2005-09-20 (ICD-10 E28.2); no current treatment documented
objective.missing: Current hormonal status, metabolic panel, and relationship to respiratory symptoms

objective.vernacular: Pulse count and number of breaths per minute at rest
objective.value: Heart rate 82 bpm (2026-06-14), 72 bpm (2026-07-02); respiratory rate not recorded

assessment_candidates.vernacular: Childhood asthma that has become inactive — no symptoms and no treatment needed as an adult
assessment_candidates.basis: Up to 50–70% of children with mild-to-moderate asthma experience clinical remission by adulthood; normal SpO2 and absence of reported symptoms are consistent with this.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Cannot confirm remission without spirometry showing normal or near-normal lung function and a thorough symptom review — remission is a diagnosis of exclusion.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: If wrongly classified as remitted, asthma exacerbations could go unrecognized and unequipped — including risk during surgery, illness, or new triggers.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: Asthma still present but mild enough that the person hasn't noticed symptoms or has adapted to them without realizing it
assessment_candidates.basis: Studies show that up to 30–40% of patients with apparent childhood asthma remission have persistent airflow limitation or bronchial hyperresponsiveness on formal testing; mild rhinitis noted in this patient.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Symptom self-report is unreliable for detecting mild persistent asthma — only objective testing can rule this in or out.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Unrecognized persistent asthma leaves the person unprotected during exacerbations and creates a medication safety risk — ibuprofen (currently used) can trigger severe bronchospasm in NSAID-sensitive asthmatics.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: A type of asthma where ibuprofen, aspirin, and similar pain medicines can trigger sudden dangerous breathing attacks
not_yet_testable: s-009 (NSAID-triggered respiratory symptoms — not yet asked)
assessment_candidates.basis: AERD occurs in approximately 10–20% of adult asthmatics; ibuprofen is a current OTC medication, making this a clinically urgent question regardless of overall asthma activity.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Risk cannot be assessed without knowing whether ibuprofen has ever worsened breathing — this is the highest-urgency gap in the current record.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: If this person has AERD and continues ibuprofen, a severe and potentially life-threatening bronchospasm could occur.

assessment_candidates.term: Allergic rhinitis with possible cough-variant asthma
assessment_candidates.vernacular: Persistent nose allergy that may be causing airway irritation and a cough that can look like asthma
assessment_candidates.basis: Allergic rhinitis and asthma share the same atopic inflammatory pathway; rhinitis noted at visit; cough-variant asthma may present without wheeze in adults.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Rhinitis may be purely infectious given it was noted at a single visit — needs chronicity and trigger data to assess.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: If untreated, ongoing allergic airway inflammation can impair quality of life and progress to worsening asthma control.

assessment_candidates.term: Misdiagnosis — childhood diagnosis was not true asthma
assessment_candidates.vernacular: The breathing problems as a child may have been caused by something other than asthma — such as vocal cord problems, recurrent infections, or other conditions that mimic asthma
not_yet_testable: s-010 (childhood asthma history detail — not yet asked)
assessment_candidates.basis: Population studies suggest 20–30% of childhood asthma diagnoses may be incorrect or overdiagnosed; without documentation of the original workup this cannot be excluded.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Cannot assess without knowing how the original diagnosis was made and whether formal testing was done at that time.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: If the diagnosis was never correct, continued labeling affects medication decisions, insurance, and unnecessary anxiety without benefit.

assessment_candidates.term: Obesity-related dyspnea masking or mimicking asthma
assessment_candidates.vernacular: Excess weight can make breathing feel harder and cause breathlessness that is mistaken for asthma
not_yet_testable: s-012 (dyspnea at rest — not yet asked)
assessment_candidates.basis: Prior overweight diagnosis in the record; obesity causes restrictive ventilatory pattern and exertional dyspnea that may coexist with or obscure asthma; weight 185 lbs noted.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: BMI calculation is uncertain due to a likely data entry error for height; this candidate cannot be fully assessed until accurate anthropometrics are obtained.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: If obesity-related dyspnea is mistaken for asthma, the real driver (weight) goes unaddressed and the person may be unnecessarily medicated.

residual.vernacular: Something not on this list — the differential is never closed

plan_options.vernacular: Inform the patient now that ibuprofen may not be safe for someone with a history of asthma and to stop or hold it until asthma status is clarified
plan_options.basis: NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease can cause severe bronchospasm; ibuprofen is currently being used; this is the highest-urgency actionable gap in the record.
plan_options.who_can_act: Any clinician, pharmacist, or care coordinator who has access to the patient

plan_options.vernacular: Ask the patient directly about current wheeze, exercise symptoms, nocturnal symptoms, triggers, and childhood asthma details
plan_options.basis: Clinical guidelines (GINA 2024) require symptom history as the foundation of asthma status assessment; most subjective fields in this frame are absent.
plan_options.who_can_act: Clinician, nurse, or trained care coordinator at the next contact

plan_options.vernacular: A breathing test before and after an inhaler to see whether airflow is normal and whether any obstruction reverses
plan_options.basis: GINA 2024 and NICE NG80 recommend spirometry as the objective standard for confirming or ruling out current asthma; cannot confirm remission without it.
plan_options.who_can_act: Ordering clinician (physician or advanced practice provider); performed in pulmonary function lab or equipped primary care office

plan_options.vernacular: A quick, non-invasive breath test that measures airway inflammation and helps identify allergic asthma even without symptoms
plan_options.basis: FeNO ≥25 ppb supports eosinophilic airway inflammation; useful when spirometry is normal but asthma is still suspected (GINA 2024).
plan_options.who_can_act: Ordering clinician; performed in pulmonary function lab or specialist office

plan_options.term: Allergen sensitization testing — serum IgE and RAST panel
plan_options.vernacular: Blood tests to find out whether the immune system is reacting to dust mites, pollens, mold, or pet dander
plan_options.basis: Identifies atopic phenotype; guides both rhinitis and asthma management; relevant given rhinitis symptom noted.

plan_options.term: Asthma action plan — stand-by prescription if confirmed active
plan_options.vernacular: If testing shows asthma is still present, provide a written plan and a rescue inhaler prescription before the next visit
plan_options.basis: GINA 2024 recommends all patients with confirmed active asthma have a written action plan and access to short-acting bronchodilator.
plan_options.who_can_act: Prescribing clinician (physician or advanced practice provider)

plan_options.vernacular: Get a measured height and weight to calculate the correct BMI — the height in the record (220 cm / 7'3") appears to be a data entry error
plan_options.basis: Accurate anthropometrics are needed to assess weight-related contributions to respiratory symptoms and to reconcile the conflicting overweight diagnosis and low calculated BMI.
plan_options.who_can_act: Any clinical staff member at next in-person visit
